'''Joseph Percival Allen IV''' (born June 27, 1937) is an American former [[NASA]] [[astronaut]]. He logged more than 3,000 hours flying time in [[jet aircraft]].

==Early life and education==
Allen was born in [[Crawfordsville, Indiana]], in June 1937. His parents, Mr. and Mrs. Joseph P. Allen III, had resided in [[Frankfort, Indiana]]. He attended Mills School, and is a graduate of [[Crawfordsville High School]] in Indiana, Class of 1955; received a Bachelor of Arts degree in Mathematics and Physics from [[DePauw University]] in 1959, where he was a member of Delta chapter of [[Beta Theta Pi]],<ref>[http://www.depauw.edu/news/index.asp?id=15786 "Joe Allen '59 Enters US Astronaut Hall of Fame"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060920085342/http://www.depauw.edu/news/index.asp?id=15786 |date=September 20, 2006 }}, DePauw University News, May 1, 2005</ref> and Master of Science and PhD degrees in Physics from [[Yale University]] in 1961 and 1965,<ref name="thesis-allen-1965">{{cite thesis |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/302190487 |title=Studies of odd-A nuclei in the 2S-1D shell |date=1965 |publisher=[[Yale University]] |type=Ph.D. |last=Allen |first=Joseph Percival IV |id={{ProQuest|302190487 }} |url-access=subscription|oclc=162101874}}</ref> respectively. At Yale, Allen worked with future physicist [[Richard F. Casten]].<ref name="Zierler">{{cite web |last=Zierler |first=David |date=June 25, 2020 |title=Interview of Richard Casten |url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/46761 |access-date=November 27, 2023 |website=Niels Bohr Library & Archives |publisher=[[American Institute of Physics]] |archive-date=November 28, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231128040802/https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/46761 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Allen was a research associate in the Nuclear Physics Laboratory at the [[University of Washington]] prior to his selection as an astronaut. He was a staff physicist at the Nuclear Structure Laboratory at Yale University in 1965 and 1966, and during the period 1963 to 1967, was a guest researcher at [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]].

==NASA experience==
Allen was selected as a scientist-astronaut by NASA in August 1967 as a member of the second group of [[Astronaut group 6|scientist-astronauts]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/30779535/muncie_evening_press/|title=New Citizens to be Astros|newspaper=Muncie Evening Press|location=Muncie, Indiana|date=August 3, 1967|page=19|via=Newspapers.com|agency=UPI|archive-date=April 30, 2019|access-date=April 20, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190430040630/https://www.newspapers.com/clip/30779535/muncie_evening_press/|url-status=live}}</ref> He completed flight training at [[Vance Air Force Base]], [[Oklahoma]]. He was mission scientist while a member of the astronaut support crew for [[Apollo 15]] and was a staff consultant on science and technology to the President's Council on International Economic Policy.

From August 1975 to 1978, Allen was NASA Assistant Administrator for Legislative Affairs in Washington, D.C. Returning to the [[Johnson Space Center]] in 1978, as a senior scientist astronaut, Allen was assigned to the Operations Mission Development Group. He was a support crew member for the first orbital flight test of the [[Space Shuttle]] (''[[Space Shuttle Columbia|Columbia]]'') in April 1981 and was the [[Capsule communicator|CAPCOM]] during the reentry phase for this mission. In addition, in 1980 and 1981, he worked as the technical assistant to the director of flight operations.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/allen_joseph_p.pdf|title=Joseph P. Allen (Ph.D.) NASA Astronaut (Former)|date=December 1993|access-date=January 8, 2021|publisher=NASA|archive-date=May 31, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220531032806/https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/allen_joseph_p.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Space experience==
[[File:STS-5 Allen EVA training.jpg|thumb|left|Allen training for planned STS-5 spacewalk]]
Allen was mission specialist on [[STS-5]], the first fully operational flight of the [[Space Shuttle program]], which launched from [[Kennedy Space Center]], [[Florida]], on November 11, 1982. He was accompanied by [[Vance D. Brand]] (spacecraft commander), Col. [[Robert F. Overmyer]] (pilot), and Dr. [[William B. Lenoir]] (mission specialist). STS-5, the first mission with four crewmembers, clearly demonstrated the [[Space Shuttle]] as fully operational by the successful first deployment of two commercial communications [[satellite]]s from the Orbiter's payload bay. The mission marked the first use of the [[Payload Assist Module]] (PAM-D), and its new ejection system. Numerous flight tests were performed throughout the mission to document Shuttle performance during launch, boost, orbit, atmospheric entry and landing phases. STS-5 was the last flight to carry the [[Development Flight Instrumentation]] (DFI) package to support flight testing. A Getaway Special, three Student Involvement Projects, and medical experiments were included on the mission. A planned [[spacewalk]] by Allen and Lenoir, the first of the Space Shuttle program, was postponed by one day after Lenoir became ill, and then had to be canceled when the two [[spacesuit]]s that were to be used developed problems.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.spaceflightnow.com/shuttle/sts122/080210fd4/index.html|title=Mission controllers release revised flight plan|last=Harwood|first=William|publisher=Spaceflight Now|date=February 10, 2008|accessdate=June 21, 2013|archive-date=May 8, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160508003420/http://spaceflightnow.com/shuttle/sts122/080210fd4/index.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The STS-5 crew successfully concluded the 5-day orbital flight of [[Space Shuttle Columbia|Space Shuttle ''Columbia'']] with the first entry and landing through a cloud deck to a hard-surface runway and demonstrated maximum braking. STS-5 completed 81 orbits of the Earth in 122 hours before landing on a concrete runway at [[Edwards Air Force Base]], [[California]], on November 16, 1982.

[[File:STS-51-A crew.jpg|thumb|right|Allen (standing at right) with the crew of STS-51-A]]
Allen was a mission specialist on [[STS 51-A]], which launched from Kennedy Space Center, Florida, on November 8, 1984. He was accompanied by Captain [[Frederick (Rick) Hauck]] (spacecraft commander), Captain [[David M. Walker (astronaut)|David M. Walker]] (pilot), and fellow mission specialists, Dr. [[Anna Lee Fisher]] and Commander [[Dale Gardner]]. This was the second flight of the Orbiter ''[[Space Shuttle Discovery|Discovery]]''.  During the mission the crew deployed two satellites, Canada's Anik D-2 (Telesat H) and Hughes' LEASAT-1 (Syncom IV-1), and operated the [[3M Company]]'s Diffusive Mixing of Organic Solutions experiment. In the first space salvage attempt in history, Allen and Gardner performed spacewalks and successfully retrieved for return to Earth the [[Palapa B-2]] and [[Westar]] VI communications satellites. STS 51-A completed 127 orbits of the Earth in 192 hours before landing at Kennedy Space Center, Florida, on November 16, 1984. With the completion of this flight Allen logged a total of 314 hours in space.

==Post-NASA experience==
Allen was chief executive officer of [[Space Industries Incorporated|Space Industries International]], Washington, D.C., and later was chairman of [[General Dynamics|Veridian]], until he retired in 2004. [[General Dynamics]] announced its acquisition of Veridian on June 9, 2003.

In the 1998 [[HBO]] miniseries ''[[From the Earth to the Moon (miniseries)|From the Earth to the Moon]]'', Allen was played by [[Doug McKeon]].

In the 1998 movie ''[[Armageddon (1998 film)|Armageddon]]'', directed by [[Michael Bay]], Allen was a NASA consultant and cameoed as "Kennedy Launch" during the launching of the X-71 shuttles.  Allen was presented [[Indiana_State_Awards#Sagamore_of_the_Wabash|Sagamore of the Wabash]], the top award from the state of [[Indiana]], by U.S. Representative [[Jim Baird (politician)|Jim Baird]] and State Representative [[Beau Baird]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-10-15 |title=State Rep. Baird presents local retired astronaut Joseph P. Allen with Sagamore of the Wabash |url=https://www.indianahouserepublicans.com/news/press-releases/state-rep.-baird-presents-local-retired-astronaut-joseph-p.-allen-with-sagamore-of-the-wabash/ |access-date=2025-07-14 |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Allen married Bonnie Jo Darling of [[Elkhart, Indiana]] in 1961. They have two children. Bonnie Darling died in early 2021.<ref>{{cite web |title=Bonnie Allen Obituary (1939–2021) – Washington, IN – The Elkhart Truth |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/elkharttruth/name/bonnie-allen-obituary?id=20954763 |website=Legacy.com}}</ref>

==Works==
* ''Entering Space: An Astronaut's Odyssey'' (1985) {{ISBN|0-941434-74-5}}

Allen was a contributor to the book ''NASA's Scientist-Astronauts'' by David Shayler and [[Colin Burgess (author)|Colin Burgess]].

==Organizations==
Allen is a member of several organizations, including the [[American Physical Society]], the [[American Astronautical Society]], the [[American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics]], the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], [[Phi Beta Kappa]], [[Beta Theta Pi]], [[Sigma Xi]], and [[Phi Eta Sigma]].

==Special honors==
[[File:Joseph Allen Spotmeter (S82-39790).jpg|thumb|Allen performing Earth observation on STS-5 in 1982]]
* [[Fulbright Scholarship]] (1959–1960)
* Outstanding Flying Award, Class 69–06, Vance Air Force Base (1969)
* Two [[NASA Group Achievement Award]]s (1971 and 1974) in recognition of contributions to the Apollo 15 Lunar Traverse Planning Team and for subsequent work on the Outlook for Space Study Team
* Yale Science and Engineering Association Award for Advancement of Basic and Applied Science (1972)
* DePauw University Distinguished Alumnus Award (1972)
* [[NASA Exceptional Scientific Achievement Medal]] (1973)
* [[NASA Exceptional Service Medal]] (1978)
* [[NASA Superior Performance Award]] (1975 and 1981)
* Honorary Doctor of Science from DePauw University (1983)<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/29891621/the_indianapolis_news/|title=DePauw Grads Hear Trudeau|newspaper=The Indianapolis News|location=Indianapolis, Indiana|date=May 23, 1983|page=11|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>
* Komarov Diploma from the [[Fédération Aéronautique Internationale]]
* Indiana Aviation Hall of Fame, 2024 [https://inahof.org/members/2024-class/joseph-allen/ Joseph Allen]
* [[Indiana_State_Awards#Sagamore_of_the_Wabash|Sagamore of the Wabash]] 2024 [https://www.suncommercial.com/banner_graphic/archives/article_7afce89a-d4f9-5bd4-bc0e-82a04e4aec0e.html Back home again in Indiana, astronaut Joe Allen awarded Sagamore of Wabash]

Allen was one of three shuttle astronaut inducted into the [[U.S. Astronaut Hall of Fame]] in 2005.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/16059250/the_los_angeles_times/|title=Hall of Fame Inducts McCandless, 1st Untethered Astronaut|newspaper=Los Angeles Times|location=Los Angeles, California|date=May 1, 2005|page=34|via=Newspapers.com|agency=Associated Press}}</ref>
